tex_content.html:
Lemma
[Bounds on the spectrum of a symmetric operator] ↗ def:adjoint-symmetric-operator ↗ def:resolvent-set-spectrum-appendix-d ↗ thm:lax-milgram-theorem ↗ lem:cauchy-schwarz-inequality 1. appD:D.6-lem-1\group Fredholm Theory

(i) $\sigma (S)\subset [m,M]$;

(ii) $m,M\in \sigma (S)$.
Proof

\sketch If $\eta >M$, then

\[ ((\eta I-S)u,u)\geq (\eta -M)\| u\| ^2. \]

The Lax–Milgram theorem (subsection thm:lax-milgram-theorem) makes $\eta I-S$ bijective, so $\eta \in \rho (S)$. Applying the same argument to $S-\eta I$ when $\eta <m$ proves (i).

For the upper endpoint, the symmetric form $[u,v]=((MI-S)u,v)$ is nonnegative. Cauchy–Schwarz (equation lem:cauchy-schwarz-inequality) for this form gives

\[ (6)\qquad \| (MI-S)u\| \leq C((MI-S)u,u)^{1/2}. \]

Choose unit vectors $u_k$ with $(Su_k,u_k)\to M$. Then (6) gives $(MI-S)u_k\to 0$. If $M\in \rho (S)$, boundedness of $(MI-S)^{-1}$ would force $u_k\to 0$, contradicting $\| u_k\| =1$. Thus $M\in \sigma (S)$. Applying the same argument to the nonnegative form $((S-mI)u,v)$ proves $m\in \sigma (S)$.

□
